young.html: John Maynard Keynes (say KAYNZ) was a British economist. In the 1930s, during the Great Depression, millions of people who wanted to work could not find jobs. Keynes asked: why would a whole country get stuck like that?

His idea, in simple form: one person's spending is another person's income. If everyone gets scared and stops spending at once, shops sell less, so they hire fewer workers, who then have less to spend, and so on. Spending travels around a town in a chain. When the chain slows, the whole town slows.

young.name: gb-keynes-multiplier
young.cap: Watch \$100 of new spending travel around a town. Each person spends part of what they receive and saves the rest. (A simple model.)

young.html: Other economists disagreed with Keynes about what to do, and their side is in the lesson too.

The spending chain game. Give the first player 20 paper coins. Each player keeps a quarter of what they receive (rounding down) and passes the rest to the next player. Keep going until less than one coin is passed. Add up everything that was passed along. Was it more than 20? Why?

full.html: John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946) taught economics at Cambridge, worked for the British Treasury, and became famous in 1919 with The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which warned that the harsh treaty after the First World War would harm Europe. The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money appeared in February 1936, in the depths of the Great Depression. In 1944 Keynes led the British delegation at Bretton Woods, which designed the postwar money system.
No excerpts here. The General Theory was first published in 1936 and is under copyright in the U.S. This lesson explains its ideas in our own words. It is in most libraries.

The economics Keynes learned held that markets tend to correct themselves: if workers are unemployed, wages fall until employers hire them again, and whatever people earn they either spend or save, and savings are lent out and spent on investment. A famous form of this is Say's law, often summed up as "supply creates its own demand." Yet in the 1930s unemployment stayed very high for years.

Keynes argued that total output and employment depend on aggregate demand: the total spending of households, businesses and government. If people decide to spend less and save more, and businesses, uncertain about the future, do not invest those savings, total spending falls. Then output and jobs fall, and the economy can settle at high unemployment with no automatic force to lift it out. Wages may be slow to fall, and even if they fall, workers' spending falls with them.

head: Idea
Keynes's point (our summary)
rows: People spend part of any rise in income and save the rest; the part spent is the marginal propensity to consume (MPC).
New spending becomes someone's income, part of which is spent again, so the total rise in income is larger than the first spending.
Interest is the reward for giving up holding ready money; in a slump, people may hoard cash rather than lend or invest.
Investment depends on confidence and expectations, which can swing widely.
If everyone tries to save more at once, total spending and income can fall, so total saving may not rise.

full.name: gb-keynes-multiplier
full.cap: The multiplier: spending, round by round.

full.title: The multiplier
full.q: If the marginal propensity to consume is 0.8, how much can total income rise from \$100 of new spending, in the simple model?
steps: Each round, people spend 0.8 of what they receive: \$100, then \$80, then \$64, and so on.
The sum of this series is $\frac{1}{1 - 0.8} = 5$ times the first spending.

full.html: From this Keynes drew a policy conclusion: in a deep slump, governments should support demand, for example by spending on public works, even if that means borrowing, and should keep interest rates low.

The General Theory changed economics, and for about thirty years after the Second World War many governments used Keynesian ideas to manage demand. It was always debated. Friedrich Hayek and the Austrian school argued that slumps come from earlier misdirected investment that has to be worked out, and that government spending can prolong the problem. Milton Friedman and the monetarists argued that the Great Depression was made far worse by a collapse in the money supply, and that steady growth of money matters more than government spending. In the 1970s many countries had high inflation and high unemployment at once ("stagflation"), which simple Keynesian models had not predicted. Robert Lucas and others argued that people's expectations adjust to policy, weakening its effects, and public-choice economists such as James Buchanan warned that governments find it easier to borrow than to repay. Today most economists combine parts of these views: many accept that demand matters in the short run and that markets adjust over the long run, and they disagree about how large the multiplier is and when policy should act.

Thinking Keynes wanted governments to spend more all the time. He argued for supporting demand in slumps, not for permanent deficits; in his later writings he favored balancing the government's ordinary budget over time.

items: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations, in the 18th-century rungs, set out how markets coordinate economic life; Keynes asked why that coordination can fail for a whole economy.
Marx's Capital also saw slumps as built into capitalism, but Keynes wanted to save the market system, not replace it.
Veblen and Tawney, earlier rungs, criticized the motives of a money economy; Keynes focused on how it works as a machine.

The Economics Ladder topics on aggregate demand, the multiplier and schools of thought teach the models built from these debates; the American History topics on the Great Depression and the New Deal show the times.

questions: How is your spending someone else's income? Follow a dollar through three people.
